Partially Stabilized Zirconia (PSZ) may become widely used for Thermal Barrier Coatings (TBC).
Failure of PSZ coatings can occur due to thermal fatigue in oxidizing atmospheres.
The failure is caused by the strains that develop due to thermal gradients, differences in thermal expansion coefficient, and oxidation of the bond coating.
A new X-ray diffraction technique is used to accurately determine the fraction of cubic, tetragonal, and monoclinic phases in PSZ coatings.

The phase transformations between the cubic, tetragonal, and monoclinic phases in PSZ coatings during thermal cycling lead to the development of strains and stresses that contribute to the failure of the coatings.

Strategies to improve the life of PSZ thermal barrier coatings include increasing the toughness through transformation toughening, improving the thermal expansion match, and using an oxidation-resistant bond coating.
The as-sprayed PSZ coatings had 91.9% cubic, 3.0% tetragonal, and 5.1% monoclinic phases.
The thermally cycled PSZ coatings had 80.0% cubic, 20.1% tetragonal, and 0.0% monoclinic phases.
The (400) peak region in the X-ray diffraction pattern is used to separate the tetragonal and cubic phases in PSZ.
The theoretical value for the intensity ratio (111)/(400) in the X-ray diffraction pattern is 3.15, indicating a texture effect in the coatings.
